resources.string: Hoverboard Remote needs Bluetooth access to scan for and connect to your board. This is required to drive the vehicle. No location data is collected.
The board would not attach. It may be armed; power-cycle it and try again.
Not in the list? Reach a board by name.
Hold the throttle to drive · release to stop
Tap ARM to enable the motors
Bound: both boards get this demand · release to stop
Differential: up to drive, sideways to turn · release to stop
Rigid body: up to lean, sideways to turn · release to stop
Both boards are set to one rigid machine, but neither is running as its leader yet. Set both to Balance under Drive on the Setup tab, and arm once so a new setting takes hold.
THE TWO BOARDS ARE SET TO DIFFERENT FRAMES
BOTH BOARDS ARE SET AS THE RIGHT WHEEL
NEITHER BOARD IS SET AS THE RIGHT WHEEL
The app disarmed this machine when it stopped being on screen. Nothing faulted and the board is still connected. Tap to arm again.
Rider requirement waived: in balance mode, arming engages. Hold the frame upright when arming.
Rider requirement may be waived: the app cannot tell what the board is running. In balance mode, arming may engage. Hold the frame upright when arming.

The two boards are set to different frames: the master to %1$s and the slave to %2$s. One wheel would try to balance the machine and the other would freewheel. Set both the same under Machine on the Setup tab.
The app has not read the frame setting on both boards, so it cannot tell whether they match. Open Setup and tap Read again.
Only one board has been found, so the app cannot tell whether this machine\'s two boards are set to the same frame. If it has a second board, power it and reconnect.
Neither board is set as the right wheel, so a turn would come out mirrored. Pick the right wheel under Machine on the Setup tab.
Both boards are set as the right wheel, so a turn would come out wrong. Pick one of them under Machine on the Setup tab.
The app has not read which board is the right wheel on both boards. Open Setup and tap Read again.
No fault producer is asserted on the board this phone is attached to. That is one board\'s own producers; the other board has its own chip above, so this cannot clear the machine.
This board is reporting no pack voltage. Either it does not sense the rail, or its motor has not been brought up.
No charge figure: nobody has told this machine how many cells its pack has. Set it under Setup, in Drive.
no total while a board is not reporting
motors off, no current to measure
Figures rest on each board\'s own calibration, which has not been checked against a meter yet, and leave out the 0.08 A each board draws for itself.
The board switches between these two by itself, by whether anybody is on the pads; the chips only pick which set you are editing. %1$s
Somebody is on the pads now, so it is on the %1$s set.
The pads are clear now, so it is on the %1$s set.
Waiting for telemetry to say which set it is on now.
The slave does not report its rider level, so which set it is on now is not known here.
%1$s But the rider requirement may be waived on this board, and a board running waived stays on the %2$s set whatever the pads say.
This board does not require a rider, so the balance loop always runs the one set of gains below.
These gains never hold the machine up: the board does not engage on this set. What they shape is the step off, where the loop ramps towards them as the rider leaves.
The slave\'s gain sets follow the rider requirement read from its store, taken to be what it runs: the board does not report the value it booted with.
These are the values last read from this board. Writes are off until it is read again.
~ converging: the loop reaches the staged value within %1$s s of the change, while it runs
Staged: the board\'s RAM value, which this slider writes. The running loop ramps to it.
Engaged: what the balance loop is using now. The board does not report it; it converges to staged over time and never jumps while the loop runs.
Flash: what a reboot restores. Only Save writes it.
~ converging: the ramp\'s bound since the last change has not elapsed. A bound, not a reading.
* unsaved: staged differs from flash. A reboot reverts to flash.
After each engage the loop starts with kp and bk at staged and ramps pr up from 0, within %1$s s. The board does not report when it engages.
Save writes flash, which the board refuses while armed. The gain sliders and Revert work armed.
Save is refused while armed. Disarm first.
The board refused %1$s: outside the range it accepts.
The board does not know %1$s as a tunable gain (its firmware may predate the tune lane).
%1$s: wrote %2$s, the board reports %3$s. Read again.
No answer about %1$s. The board may be out of reach, or its firmware may predate the tune lane.
The link is busy with another read; try again.
The board\'s answer about %1$s was not understood.
No board attached; nothing was sent.

An outer loop that sits over the gains above: with it running, the stick asks for a SPEED and the loop picks the lean that holds it, which is what makes the machine hold a hill and come back to a stop on its own. These three are RAM values like the gains, so Save is what keeps them; without it a power cycle brings back the flash value each row shows.
Off: speed_kp is 0, so the loop does not run and the stick commands lean directly.
Running: the stick commands speed, and the loop sets the lean that holds it. Set speed_kp to 0 to turn it off and go back to commanding lean.
Not read from this board yet.
Armed: these three work armed, like the gains. Moving speed_kp between 0 and anything else swaps what the stick commands, so make that one change stopped.
speed_kp (hundredths of a degree of lean per count of speed error)
How hard the loop leans to answer a speed error, and the loop\'s own off switch: 0 turns the whole thing off. Around 100 brings the machine back to the asked-for speed in about 1.7 seconds.
speed_ki (hundredths of a degree of lean per count-second)

Takes out the standing error a slope leaves. 0 clears the stored-up correction on the spot, which is how a wound-up one is dumped without disarming. The larger it is, the less the machine rolls before it parks on a hill.
speed_max (sixteenths of a count at full stick)

How fast a full stick asks to go: 16 is one count, which is roughly 0.287 m/s if the wheel is the 165 mm one this figure assumes, and 80 is about walking pace. 0 is a working setting and not a broken one: the machine holds its place and the stick does nothing.
0 to %1$s, the same on every board: this limit is built into the firmware rather than stored on the board.
Type a whole number from 0 to %1$s.

How far the stick may lean and turn the machine. These are stored on the board, unlike the gains above, so each one is written when you let go of its slider and the board starts using it the next time it is armed.
Armed: these four are stored values and the board refuses to store anything while armed. Disarm below to change them, then arm again.

How far the machine leans away from upright with the stick all the way forward: 600 is six degrees. The more it may lean, the harder it accelerates. 0 ignores the stick and the machine only holds itself up.
Lean rate (hundredths of a degree per step)
How far the lean may move in one control step. The boards take %1$d steps a second, so 12 swings the lean by 30 degrees in a second, and 4 by ten degrees.

How hard the two wheels are driven apart with the stick all the way over, in the counts the wheels take torque in, where the top of the range below is everything one wheel has. 0 drives straight and ignores steering. Only a machine set to one rigid frame steers at all.
How far the turn may move in one control step. The boards take %1$d steps a second, so against a 12000 turn limit, 240 reaches full lock in a fifth of a second and 24 takes two seconds.
A stored limit cannot be written while armed. Disarm first.
%1$s is outside what the board keeps, so nothing was sent.
The same stick and arm control as the Ride screen, on the same board.
The board refuses every settings write while it is armed. Disarm on the Ride tab to edit.
The board answered with something this app could not read.
Takes effect the next time the board is armed.
Takes effect the next time the board starts up.
Takes effect here at once. The board stores this one for the app and never acts on it itself.
Not a value this field takes
Too long: at most %1$d bytes fit one write
Stored byte %1$s is none of these
Armed: read only. The board refuses a write to this field.
Written. The board has not restarted since, so it is still running the old value.
The board refused this write: it is armed.
The board refused this write as malformed.
The board does not know this field.
The board stores this field as a different type.
The board could not store this (flash full or failed).
The board is out of space for configuration, so this was not stored.
The board could not commit its compacted configuration page, so this was not stored.
No answer from the board. It was read again to see what it holds.
The answer from the board could not be understood.
The link was busy with another request, so nothing was written.
No board attached, so nothing was written.
Not written: the other board had to be set to the left wheel first, and that write did not land.
The stored orientation is not whole

The stored IMU orientation is not a proper rotation, or part of it cannot be read while some of it was just written. That happens when writing a frame stopped part way, and a board can also hold such a frame from before this session. The board refuses to arm on it, and started up on it does not bring its IMU up at all, so it cannot balance either way. Pick a pose below: the whole frame is written again, and this warning goes once the stored frame is whole.

Writing the orientation: eight fields, one write each. Between the two axis-role writes the board can hold the same chip axis twice, which it refuses; an arm attempted in that moment is refused once, and the arm after it takes the new frame.
The Bluetooth module takes a new name only after it is power-cycled out of data mode.
Set by the link walk; not editable here.
Six-step and sine both drive the wheel. Field-oriented control can be selected but does not turn a wheel yet, and a board whose current sensing was not calibrated at start-up falls back to six-step.
0 = unset. A configured gate group needs %1$d DTG ticks or more.
The firmware converts this through the board\'s own counts per amp, then lowers a limit above what that board\'s sense range can hold, and raises one below its sense noise.
Not required: balance engages without a rider, so arming is the engage act and the frame must be held upright when arming. The with-a-rider gains run at all times. Any byte but 0 reads as required.
0 = none. Refuses a balance engage below it, never ends a run.
0 = off, and the third gain (pr) then moves nothing. Above 0 it is not damping: the board holds a steady torque with the deck level, and pr sets how much.
0 = not set, and then the Ride screen shows pack volts with no percentage. Set the same count on both boards: one pack feeds them both. A cell counts as full at 4.2 V and empty at 3.0 V.
The largest value the Tune steppers and the board accept for this gain, in both profiles; the minimum is 0. A gain above it is clamped down to it.
1 = X, 2 = Y, 3 = Z, 0 = unset (the compiled role). Written only by the orientation pose picker above, together with the signs.
The raw byte behind the Frame control under Machine, for a bench with only one board powered. Set it the same on both boards.
The raw byte behind the Right wheel control under Machine. Exactly one board of a pair is the right wheel.
-1, +1, or 0 for unset (runs the firmware fallback for that axis). Written only by the orientation pose picker above, together with the axis roles, because one sign on its own cannot make a rotation.
no average while a board is not reporting
Travel is counted in hall edges. A distance needs the wheel\'s size, which the board has not been told.
Travel is counted in hall edges and converted here using the wheel size each board has been told.
These settings describe the whole machine rather than one board, so picking one here writes it to both boards.

Set a new machine up in this order: the right wheel, then the frame, then the control mode under Drive below, then the lean and turn limits on the Tune screen. Each one does nothing until the next is set, and the machine neither leans nor steers while those two limits are 0.

Pivoting platforms: each board balances the platform it sits under, using its own sensor. That is how a hoverboard works, and it is what a board does out of the box. Rigid body: the two wheels are bolted into one frame, the board that has the sensor balances the whole machine and tells the other wheel what to do.

Which board drives the right-hand wheel, looking the way the machine drives forward. Picking one makes the other board the left wheel, and that board is written first, so if the second write fails neither board is left on the right. Nothing is picked for you: the answer is different from machine to machine.
Neither board is the right wheel. Both are set to the left, which is how a board leaves the factory.
Both boards are set to the right wheel.
The two boards do not agree. Fix it here before riding.
No second board was found this session, so a write reaches only the attached board and the other half of each pair stays unknown.
Stand the frame level, then set. The trims that zero the current pitch and roll are written to the board.
No attitude from the board yet

Pick how the board sits in the machine: which face points up, then what points forward. The app writes both orientation fields from that choice: the axis roles (which chip axis is up, which measures the pitch rate) and the six signs. Every pose is a proper rotation; a board refuses to arm on any other frame, and one started up on such a frame does not bring its IMU up at all.

The poses assume the standard board family\'s chip mount (the measured yaw, not the firmware\'s compiled fallback). A board of another family needs its chip mount measured before these poses are right for it.
Stored as: %1$s. The board takes the stored map the next time it is armed, not now.
Unset signs and roles run the firmware fallback.
The stored frame is not a proper rotation (mirrored, or an invalid pair of roles). The board refuses to arm on it, and started up on it does not bring its IMU up at all. Pick a pose below.
Drawn with the machine\'s forward to the right and up at the top; the component side is shaded and the arrow marks the stock-forward edge.
unset (firmware fallback; reads as %1$s on this family)
The board as it runs now

Side view (forward to the right) and view from behind, tilted by the pitch and roll the board reports. Tilt the board: the drawing should tilt the same way. It shows the frame the board is running, not one that has been stored since.

Run on the assembled frame, after the arm that applies the orientation. A pass means the pitch and roll the board reports agree with its map. The up-axis gravity sign and the pitch-rate sign are not sent over Bluetooth; they need the bench check.
Frame level: pitch and roll within 10° of zero.
Hold the frame leaning forward more than 10°: pitch reads negative.
The orientation was written this session. The board re-reads the frame when it arms, so arm it once before running this check.
A sign must be -1, 0 (unset) or +1. Nothing was written.
The accelerometer signs would form a mirrored frame (determinant -1). Nothing was written.
The gyro signs would form a mirrored frame (determinant -1). Nothing was written.
The axis roles would name one chip axis twice or a value outside 0 to 3. Nothing was written.
This board has not reported its attitude.
The stored values this needs have not been read.
The board is running a value the app cannot know: a field this depends on was written this session and the board takes it up at its next arm.
The board is running a value the app cannot know: a field this depends on was written this session and the board takes it up when it restarts.
A different board attached. The edits for board %1$s were dropped.
A layout is written to flash, which the board refuses while armed. Disarm to edit it.
The layout has not been read yet.
%1$d of the layout\'s fields could not be read, so there is no layout to judge. Read again.
Part: %1$s, as the board reports it.
This board has not sent its part yet. It arrives with the board\'s state, a few times a second.
This board reports a part this app does not know.
A layout is only valid or invalid ON a part: pins that one part bonds the next one does not. So there is no verdict here, and nothing can be changed.

Applying one is the normal case: a preset is a whole layout for a board variant, so no pin has to be entered by hand. Drive direction, align offset and the current calibration are left as this board holds them: a pin map cannot state them.
This preset moves the power latch

The board holds its own power on through %1$s; this preset says %2$s. On battery, the pin is what keeps the board alive: if the wrong one is staged, the board powers itself off the moment it boots, and only a debugger attached over SWD can bring it back. Everything else in the preset is staged either way.
This layout validates. The board would accept it and bring up what it describes.
The layout has not been read, so there is nothing to judge.
The board\'s boot validator is a pure function of these fields, this part and the reserved pins, and this is that function\'s answer.

What only a reboot can tell: whether the hardware behaves, so whether the IMU answers on the staged bus, the halls read and the motors turn. The board\'s own verdict is not readable over the link either, so a clean apply is confirmed by the board behaving on reconnect.
A wrong layout disables the affected function until it is corrected and re-booted; the board stays reachable. The link\'s own pins are not layout fields and cannot be claimed by one.
The board currently STORES a layout it would refuse, on %1$s. A layout is one object, so this is an invalid board rather than a board half-way to a new layout. Finish applying the changes below.
Apply is disabled while the verdict is a refusal. There is no override: the board would refuse this layout at boot and come up link-only.
No changes staged. Edits here are local until Apply writes them.
Power-cycle the board to apply %1$d field(s). The layout is read once at boot.
The app is watching for the restart and clears this by itself, so there is nothing to confirm. The Bluetooth module goes down with the board, so the link drops and comes back.
Written, not applied: runs from the next power-up.
Direction and align offset are the Setup screen\'s rows. They are read here because a layout is one object, and they do not change the verdict.

Set by a known-good layout above, after a confirmation, and not by hand. On battery this pin is what holds the board\'s own power on, so a wrong one powers the board off at boot and only SWD can recover it.
Both pins and a model, or none: a half-staged IMU is a refused layout, not an absent IMU.
All six gates with a dead time at or above the floor, or none. The picker offers only this part\'s advanced-timer pins, and the six still have to form one timer\'s complementary set.
Both pins exactly when the sense is declared present, and both on an analog pin.
%1$d DTG ticks or more once the gates are configured; 0 only with them unset. A shorter one lets both FETs of a leg conduct.
This field could not be read.
Not editable: the board\'s part is not known.
No pin on this part is free and eligible for this function.
That byte is not a pin this encoding defines.
The function\'s fields are all-or-none and only some are set.
The gates are configured, so the dead time must be %1$d DTG ticks or more. Anything shorter is shoot-through.
%1$s is already claimed by another function.
%1$s belongs to a live link port or to SWD.
%1$s is not bonded on this part.
%1$s drives an advanced timer, so only a gate may claim it.
These six pins are not one advanced timer\'s complementary set.
%1$s has no ADC channel behind it.
Those two pins are not a hardware I2C bus. A software bus is not built.
The stored IMU orientation is not a rotation. The Setup screen owns it.
The board is armed. A layout is written to flash, which it refuses while armed.
No board is attached, so nothing was sent.
The board\'s part is not known, so there is no verdict to apply against.
That layout is one the board would refuse, so it was not written.
The link was busy with another request, so nothing was sent.
The write to %1$s went unanswered. The board may or may not hold it; the field was read back.
The board answered the write to %1$s with something the protocol does not define.
The board refused the write to %1$s.
A different board attached. The layout read from board %1$s was dropped: pins are a fact about one board.
